_comments.aggregationMethod: numberOfRuns raised from 2 to 5 and assert.aggregationMethod set explicitly to "median" as an anti-flake measure for the shared GitHub Actions runner, NOT a threshold weakening (minScore values are untouched). This was verified against the @lhci/utils 0.15.1 source, not assumed: the LHCI default aggregationMethod is "optimistic", which for a minScore assertion already takes Math.max(...values) across runs (best-case run wins) -- so a single low outlier (e.g. the 0.64 LCP run seen in run 31521650034) was already being discarded before this change; the assertion still failed because the *best* run (0.93) was below the 0.95 gate, not because of the outlier alone. "median-run" (whole-LHR representative-run selection via FCP/TTI proximity) was considered but does NOT work for categories:* assertions: LHCI's getCategoryAssertionResults always reads raw per-run category scores regardless of aggregationMethod, and getValueForAggregationMethod only special-cases the literal string "median" -- "median-run" falls through to the same Math.max behavior as the default. Only aggregationMethod: "median" actually computes the statistical median of the 5 raw performance-category scores for the /pt and /pt/link-charts assertions.
_comments.performance-floor-decision: 2026-08-11: Bruno decided the `categories:performance` floor is 0.85 on /pt (home) and 0.9 on /pt/link-charts, superseding the 0.95 default for these two pages specifically. Root cause is shared for both: the shared 2-core GitHub Actions runner used by this CI job measures meaningfully lower and noisier scores than local hardware or production. On /pt, the real median observed across GH Actions runs is ~0.89, but individual runs oscillate 0.57-0.95 -- this runner is too noisy for a 0.90 floor to hold reliably (the prior 0.9 floor sat right on top of the median and flaked red on ordinary variance, not real regressions); the home page also mounts all 9 skill categories in the DOM at once (see the 1aacb26 fix keeping all skill categories mounted for crawlers/ATS) so search engines and applicant-tracking systems can read them, which is a deliberate SEO trade-off that costs some runtime/render performance headroom on a constrained runner. 0.85 is calibrated to sit safely below that ~0.89 median while still catching a real regression (a sustained drop, not single-run noise). On /pt/link-charts the measured median is 0.94, a comfortable margin above its 0.9 floor (see performance-link-charts below for the full history), so that page's gate is unchanged. This is not a claim about production quality -- Vercel's edge network is expected to score >=95 on both pages, and that will be verified against the live production deployment after each deploy, separately from this CI gate. accessibility, best-practices and the per-audit SEO assertions are untouched and remain strict (0.95 / 1.0) on both pages.
_comments.canonical: The only failing SEO audit on both pages is `canonical` (score 0, 'Points to another hreflang location'). It's a false positive of auditing http://localhost:*: the page's rel=canonical correctly points at https://brunocordeiro.dev (production), so Lighthouse flags a mismatch against the localhost origin it's actually crawling. Production canonical/SEO is unaffected (SEO audit is 100 against the real domain). Rather than lower the aggregate `categories:seo` gate to hide this, `canonical` is disabled per URL and every other SEO audit that IS valid on localhost is asserted individually at error/minScore 1, so a real regression (missing title, bad robots.txt, non-crawlable links, missing alt text, etc.) still fails the build. `structured-data` is intentionally not asserted: it's a `manual` (unscored) Lighthouse audit and asserting minScore on it always fails LHCI with 'audit did not produce a value'.
_comments.performance-link-charts: /pt/link-charts is a content-dense case-study page (long-form prose, a syntax-highlighted-ready terminal transcript, and a whileInView pipeline animation), unlike the mostly-above-the-fold home page. It was optimized (see PipelineDiagramLazy), and the hero (title/tagline/CTA) no longer sits behind Reveal's whileInView fade — that section now paints visible on first load instead of waiting on a scroll-triggered IntersectionObserver, which was hiding the LCP element behind an animation. After that fix, 3 local runs at :3002 on this dev machine landed stably at 0.94/0.94/0.94 (median 0.94), up from the ~0.91-0.94 range and the 0.88 previously measured on the GitHub Actions runner used for the Lighthouse job. 0.94 local is still short of a *stable* 0.95, and this machine's local numbers have historically run a few points above what the shared 2-core GitHub Actions runner produces, so `minScore: 0.95` is not restored yet. 0.9 is the new evidence-based floor: the highest value that stays safely below the measured local median while remaining meaningfully higher than the previous 0.85 floor, so it still fails the build on a real regression. This is a tracked, intentional deviation from the project's default 0.95 performance gate — whether to push further (e.g. re-attempt 0.95 after further optimization, or accept 0.9 permanently) is a call for Bruno, not this fix. Production on Vercel's edge network measures meaningfully faster than this CI job's localhost `next start` run, so this threshold is specific to this gate, not a claim about production performance. a11y, best-practices and the per-audit SEO gates above remain strict (0.95 / 1.0) for this page.
